candidateRows: Historians' differing horizons inevitably shape their interpretations and prevent consensus about the historical Jesus.
This methodological claim explains why scholars reach divergent conclusions from shared evidence and frames Licona's approach throughout the dialogue.
Licona opens by comparing historical judgment to politically divided interpretation, arguing that every historian views evidence through personally conditioned horizons.
Historical inquiry distinguishes the verifiable historical Jesus from the Christ of faith and the inaccessible real Jesus.
The distinction directly defines what historians can verify about Jesus while preserving a separate category for theological claims about his identity.
Licona distinguishes historically demonstrable claims from the New Testament's theological portrait and from the complete person who actually lived in antiquity.
Common-sense authenticity criteria permit historians to establish a substantial core of facts about Jesus despite interpretive disagreement.
This supplies Licona's evidentiary method and grounds his claim that baptism, ministry, extraordinary deeds, crucifixion, and death are historically recoverable.
Licona describes source proximity, eyewitness connection, embarrassment, independent attestation, and hostile testimony, then rejects abandoning such criteria merely for failing to create consensus.
Faith and history, fact and interpretation, and metaphor and literal statement must remain distinguishable but inseparable dialectical partners.
This framework underlies Crossan's historical and theological case, especially his treatment of divine titles and metaphor as reality-forming rather than merely literal description.
Crossan grounds his method in Aquinas, argues that interpretations accompany facts, and contrasts Rome's peace through victory with Jesus' peace through justice.
Mark and John contain testimony traceable to eyewitnesses, supporting the historical value of the Gospel biographies.
Eyewitness proximity is a principal foundation for Licona's confidence that Gospel reports can support historical conclusions about Jesus and his identity.
Licona argues that Papias links Mark's material to Peter and that prevailing Johannine scholarship places a disciple or disciple-derived source behind John.
Gospel redaction and divergent passion sayings prevent historians from reliably separating eyewitness recollection from each evangelist's theological interpretation.
The argument directly weakens the claim that Gospel content can be assigned confidently to eyewitness testimony and supports Crossan's interpretation-centered reading of the sources.
Licona's claim that Mark and John preserve testimony traceable to Jesus' eyewitness disciples.
Crossan argues that Matthew and Luke alter Mark and that differing last words from the cross reveal evangelists composing fitting theological portraits rather than preserving identifiable testimony.
Jesus proclaimed God's kingdom as already present through communal participation rather than presenting himself as the expected military Messiah.
This is Crossan's direct historical account of Jesus' identity and mission, opposing an interpretation centered on explicit personal claims to messiahship or divinity.
Crossan declines speculation about private self-consciousness, emphasizing instead Jesus' public kingdom message and its contrast with the era's militarized messianic expectation.
Pauline claims, early apostolic agreement, and Mark's portrayal of divine deeds indicate that Jesus claimed a uniquely divine identity.
The argument directly supports the bodily-resurrection side's central claim that the earliest sources portray Jesus as more than Messiah and as uniquely divine.
Crossan's view that Jesus emphasized God's kingdom rather than making himself or a divine identity the central message.
Licona distinguishes Jesus from deified rulers, cites creation and preexistence language in Paul, and reads Mark's forgiveness, exorcisms, nature miracles, and resurrection deeds as divine signals.
Jesus is divine as the historical incarnation and image of God's eternal nonviolent vision, not as a literally preexistent individual.
This provides Crossan's affirmative but metaphorical account of Jesus' divinity and directly distinguishes it from Licona's literal-preexistence interpretation.
Licona's argument that early Christian sources portray Jesus as the preexistent divine creator and uniquely divine Son.
Crossan accepts exalted New Testament language but identifies the eternal reality as God's dream or vision incarnated in Jesus, whom Christians see as God's image.
Historians can verify an extraordinary event such as bodily resurrection while leaving its supernatural cause historically undetermined.
The claim directly establishes Licona's methodological basis for treating bodily resurrection as historically confirmable without requiring historical proof that God caused it.
Using a hypothetical message appearing on the moon, Licona separates confirmation of an event from identification of its cause and applies that distinction to Jesus' bodily resurrection.
The Gospel raising narratives do not provide persuasive historical support that Jesus literally restored dead people to life.
This directly addresses whether historians can verify Jesus's reputed miracles and challenges a major class of evidence for supernatural identity.
Licona's challenge that Crossan was historically ruling out Jesus's ability to raise the dead.
After arguing that healing traditions may preserve social or therapeutic effects, Crossan examines the raising stories and treats John's Lazarus account as a critique of literal restoration.
The raising narratives straightforwardly depict dead individuals being restored, even if the surviving evidence does not conclusively prove those events.
The move defends the historical investigability of miracle claims and resists Crossan's nonliteral treatment of reported raisings.
Crossan's claim that the raising accounts, especially Lazarus, undermine rather than support literal restoration.
Licona reads the narratives as assertions that genuinely dead people were raised, distinguishes that reading from proving the events, and notes agreement that historians can investigate such claims.
Historians should investigate what miracle traditions signify without granting medicine unwarranted certainty or dismissing the traditions in advance.
This supplies the methodological basis for accepting historical phenomena behind miracle reports while rejecting an automatic supernatural explanation.
Licona's contention that Crossan was adjudicating reported raisings negatively while still claiming historians can investigate miracles.
Crossan cautions against treating unexplained cures as beyond medicine, urges inquiry into what traditions report, and suggests Roman domination helps explain the concentration of demoniac accounts.
Jesus rose from the dead metaphorically, and the resurrection becomes real through participation in the transformed life it calls believers to live.
This is Crossan's principal answer to the debate's resurrection question and explains the practical and communal meaning he assigns to resurrection.

Crossan contrasts Western images of Jesus leaving a tomb with Eastern depictions involving humanity, asks why resurrection rather than ascension was proclaimed, and emphasizes living a resurrected life.
Paul describes Jesus's resurrection and the future resurrection of believers as bodily transformations, not merely as metaphors for changed conduct.
The argument directly supports bodily resurrection using early Christian sources and presents that event as the truth-defining foundation of Christianity.
Crossan's assertion that Paul chiefly cared about whether Christians lived resurrection rather than whether Jesus rose bodily.
Licona invokes firstfruits, transformed bodies, the return of believers' spirits, Gospel predictions, empty-tomb and appearance claims, and early counterexplanations to defend a physical event.
Matthew's raised-saints episode exposes difficulty in treating Jesus as the sole beginning of resurrection and is better understood as symbolic portent than literal history.
The move contests the coherence of the bodily-firstfruits case by comparing Paul with Matthew and offering a literary interpretation of anomalous resurrection material.
Licona's Pauline firstfruits argument and claim that the earliest Christians consistently proclaimed a literal bodily resurrection.
Crossan argues that Matthew's sleepers complicate Jesus's chronological priority, likens the passage to ancient death portents, and maintains that general resurrection requires plurality.
Mark, John, and Paul provide early independent support for a physical resurrection, whereas Crossan's Eastern materials are substantially later and less probative.
Independent early attestation is a principal historical foundation for Licona's bodily-resurrection case and directly challenges the competing metaphorical reconstruction.
Crossan's reliance on Matthew's plurality and Eastern-style general-resurrection imagery against an individual bodily resurrection.
Licona argues that even granting debated source relationships, multiple early streams report a physical event and Paul treats resurrection as indispensable rather than optional imagery.
The Gospel evidence may reduce to fewer independent witnesses, and resurrection was chosen over ascension because it necessarily concerned more than Jesus alone.
The move attacks Licona's multiple-attestation premise while advancing Crossan's core explanation of resurrection as the inauguration of a collective event.
Licona's claim that Paul and the Gospels independently attest a physical bodily resurrection beginning uniquely with Jesus.
Crossan treats Matthew and Luke as dependent on Mark, questions John's independence in the passion narrative, and argues that first-century Jewish resurrection could not concern Jesus alone.
Early eyewitness-rooted sources support Jesus's divine status and bodily resurrection, which supplies a historical basis strong enough to sustain Christian commitment.
The closing consolidates both branches of the motion by linking Jesus's divine claims, the earliest testimony, apostolic agreement, and resurrection's existential importance.
Crossan's source-dependence objections and his proposal that resurrection should be understood collectively and metaphorically.

Licona appeals to evidence for a spiritual dimension, early testimony that Jesus creates and sustains the universe, apostolic agreement, and the costly confidence produced by a historical resurrection.
Resurrection vindicates Jesus's nonviolent resistance to imperial violence and functions as a life-directing metaphor for humanity's survival rather than private afterlife assurance.
This closing supplies Crossan's positive account of what historians can infer about Jesus and why metaphorical resurrection remains decisive for human destiny.
Licona's claim that a metaphor cannot sustain costly Christian allegiance and that only confidence in bodily resurrection can do so.
Crossan argues that people act and die for governing metaphors, reads Jesus's isolated crucifixion as evidence of nonviolent activism, and treats resurrection as God's vindication of nonviolence.
Metaphorical resurrection should not be contrasted with reality, because a metaphor can express what is most profoundly real.
This distinction defends the conceptual coherence of Crossan's resurrection position against the charge that it substitutes something unreal for a real event.
The audience member's claim that a bodily event is real and therefore more compelling than a metaphor.
An audience member argues that first-century people facing Roman divine claims would find an actual bodily resurrection more persuasive than metaphorical language.
The first-century Christian alternative to Caesar centered on rival programs of violent imperial victory and Jewish justice, with allegiance to either resting on faith.
The argument supplies Crossan's substantive account of what resurrection proclamation meant historically and relocates its force from bodily mechanics to competing visions of world order.
The audience member's contention that only a bodily resurrection could compete effectively with Roman claims about Caesar.

After correcting the opposition between metaphor and reality, Crossan reconstructs how an ordinary Roman-era hearer might compare the practical claims of an exalted Jesus with those of an exalted emperor.
The hypothetical Q source may be connected with the Aramaic sayings or oracles attributed to Matthew by Papias.
The proposed connection offers a possible early source history for sayings material, supporting historical access to traditions associated with Jesus despite acknowledged uncertainty.
The final audience question asks Licona which material assigned to Q can probably be traced to the words of Jesus, prompting an answer about Q's identity and contents.
The Beatitudes and broader Sermon on the Mount tradition probably preserve teachings attributed to Jesus because parallel material appears across several early writings.
This provides a concrete historical argument for authentic Jesus tradition based on distributed attestation rather than reliance on the Sermon on the Mount presentation alone.
Within his response about potentially authentic Q material, Licona turns from the possible identity of Q to particular teachings and their occurrence in multiple texts.
Q sayings portraying Jesus as the eschatological judge are probably authentic recollections because historians widely accept that Jesus claimed an apocalyptic Son of Man role.
The claim bears directly on historically recoverable evidence for Jesus' extraordinary identity by grounding exalted judicial authority in sayings judged likely to be authentic.
Licona concludes the final answer by moving from ethical teaching traditions to sayings in which Jesus presents himself in an end-time judicial role.
